title: Hume's Aesthetics (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
authors: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
key_findings: Hume: verdicts of taste rest on sentiment, yet some critics are better than others.
True judge: 'strong sense, united to delicate sentiment, improved by practice, perfected by comparison, and cleared of all prejudice'.
Standard of taste = joint verdict of true critics; long-run agreement (test of time).
Objections: circularity (good art defined by good critics and vice versa), ideal vs real critics, blameless disagreement from temperament and culture.
practical_applications: A critic's authority comes from practice, side-by-side comparison and removing bias: build these into the review procedure (reference sets, blind comparison).
Some disagreement is 'blameless' (audience temperament/culture) and should not be 'fixed'.
limitations: Philosophical, not empirical; entry author/revision year not recorded this session.

title: Kant's Aesthetics and Teleology (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
authors: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
key_findings: Three aesthetic judgements: agreeable (mere liking), beautiful (taste), sublime.
Judgement of beauty: disinterested pleasure, claims universal validity without concepts, 'purposiveness without purpose', exemplary necessity grounded in a sensus communis; cannot be proved by rules.
Free beauty (independent of what the object is for) vs adherent beauty (dependent on a concept of its kind/purpose); most representational art is adherent.
Criticisms: deduction dilemma, disinterestedness, formalism, unclear normativity.
practical_applications: Commercial images are adherent beauty: judge them against their purpose (sell, explain, move), not as free art.
Separate 'I like it' (agreeable) from 'it works as this kind of thing' (adherent judgement) in critique.
limitations: Philosophical; entry author/revision year not recorded this session.

title: How Nothing Became Something: White Space, Rhetoric, History, and Meaning
authors: Pracejus, J. W., Olsen, G. D., O'Guinn, T. C.
key_findings: Per abstract/press summary: white space has no inherent meaning; it means what it does because of a history (minimalist art/architecture, late-1950s corporate art).
Creative directors and ordinary consumers share a similar understanding of white space even without knowing its origin.
Related survey (Olsen, Pracejus, O'Guinn 2012, JBR; search summary): 31 creative directors use white-space ads to make ads look good and convey prestige.
practical_applications: White space reads as prestige/quality to audiences who share this visual convention; it is a learned code, so check it holds for the target audience.
limitations: Full text not read; North American samples; convention may differ in Thai discount retail culture.

title: The Space-to-Product Ratio Effect: How Interstitial Space Influences Product Aesthetic Appeal, Store Perceptions, and Product Preference
authors: Sevilla, J., Townsend, C.
key_findings: Per abstract/press summaries: more empty space around displayed products raises perceived aesthetic appeal of the products and prestige of the store, and product preference.
Alternative explanations (popularity, scarcity, messiness) were ruled out per the abstract.
One summary: low-priced products became more aesthetically appealing but not more valuable with more space.
Field sales figures differ between sources (50% revenue/shopper vs 98%); unverified.
practical_applications: Give the hero product breathing room in frame; crowding several frames into one image signals 'stock', not 'selection'.
limitations: Full text not read; JMR 53(5) per summary; retail displays, not social posts.

title: Symbolically Simple: How Simple Packaging Design Influences Willingness to Pay for Consumable Products
authors: Ton, L. A. N., Smith, R. K., Sevilla, J.
key_findings: Per The Conversation summary (read in full) and abstracts: across 1,000+ supermarket packages, rated simplicity was positively associated with price.
Experiments: simpler packaging raised willingness to pay via perceived purity (inferred fewer ingredients).
Boundaries: weaker/absent for store brands (simple = low investment); indulgence-motivated shoppers prefer complex packaging.
practical_applications: Minimal looks signal purity/premium for health, care and 'clean' categories; for indulgent/fun categories richness may sell better.
limitations: Journal article not read; US supermarket context.

title: Signaling Status with Luxury Goods: The Role of Brand Prominence
authors: Han, Y. J., Nunes, J. C., Drèze, X.
key_findings: Brand prominence = conspicuousness of logo/marks on a product (loud vs quiet).
Four groups by wealth x need for status: patricians (quiet signals to peers), parvenus (loud, dissociate from have-nots), poseurs (loud counterfeits), proletarians.
Market data: inconspicuously branded luxury goods cost more than the same maker's conspicuously branded goods (premium for understatement); counterfeits disproportionately copy loud designs.
practical_applications: Quiet branding (small logo, recognisable form/material) reads as higher-tier luxury to insiders; big logos read as aspirational/mass. Choose by audience.
limitations: US/European luxury fashion; pre-social-media data.

title: Holistic Package Design and Consumer Brand Impressions
authors: Orth, U., Malkewitz, K.
key_findings: Per abstract/summaries: package designs cluster into five holistic types - massive, contrasting, natural, delicate, nondescript.
Recommended pairing: sincere -> natural; exciting -> contrasting; competent -> delicate; sophisticated -> natural or delicate; rugged -> contrasting or massive.
Method included 160 wine bottles and 100+ design experts rating elements (per summary).
practical_applications: Use the five holistic types as a vocabulary for brand looks; 'delicate' (muted, sleek, thin) for competence/sophistication.
limitations: Full text not read; element-level definitions not verified; wine/package domain.

title: Impression Management Using Typeface Design
authors: Henderson, P. W., Giese, J. L., Cote, J. A.
key_findings: Per abstract: empirically based guidance for choosing typefaces for impressions (pleasing, engaging, reassuring, prominent) and their trade-offs.
Six underlying design dimensions: elaborate, harmony, natural, flourish, weight, compressed.
practical_applications: Describe type choices in these dimensions (e.g., 'harmony + natural, low weight' for calm/trustworthy).
limitations: Full text not read; Latin typefaces only; Thai typefaces untested.

title: Dressed for the Occasion: Font-Product Congruity in the Perception of Logotype
authors: Doyle, J. R., Bottomley, P. A.
key_findings: Per abstract: perceived font appropriateness depends on match of connotative meaning (potency, activity) between font and product, and also on the font's meaning alone.
Related 2004 study (search summary): brands in 10 categories chosen about twice as often with an appropriate font.
practical_applications: Font must 'dress for' the product: a heavy, active font on a gentle eye-care message is incongruent.
limitations: Full text not read; Latin typefaces.

title: The Taste of Typeface
authors: Velasco, C., Woods, A. T., Hyndman, S., Spence, C.
key_findings: People matched rounder typefaces with 'sweet' and more angular typefaces with 'bitter', 'salty', 'sour'.
Rounder typefaces were liked more and judged easier to read than angular ones; authors link roundness, ease of processing, liking and taste correspondence.
practical_applications: Rounded type for soft, sweet, friendly, playful messages; angular type for sharp, intense, technical ones.
limitations: Short report, online sample, 12 typefaces (10 custom); Latin script.

title: The role of typeface on taste expectations and perception: A review (accepted manuscript)
authors: Velasco, C., Hyndman, S., Spence, C.
key_findings: Reviews evidence that typeface features (roundness/angularity) correspond to taste expectations; more preferred visual features match sweetness, less preferred match bitter/sour.
Early two-typeface finding (2014) was later replicated with more typefaces, languages and countries.
practical_applications: Typeface carries sensory and emotional connotation beyond the words; pick type as part of the look, not after it.
limitations: Manuscript submitted to Food Quality and Preference (2016); final published title/year/DOI not verified this session; food domain.

title: The Stopping Power of Advertising: Measures and Effects of Visual Complexity
authors: Pieters, R., Wedel, M., Batra, R.
key_findings: Per abstract: feature complexity (dense perceptual detail: colour, edges, luminance) reduced attention to the brand and attitude toward the ad.
Design complexity (elaborate creative arrangement of objects, shapes, patterns) increased attention to the picture and the ad, comprehension and ad attitude.
249 eye-tracked ads.
practical_applications: Cut raw clutter (noise, many small details, many colours) but keep a rich, structured design idea; 'cluttered' and 'well-designed complex' are different.
limitations: Full text not read; print ads in magazines.

title: Predicting Users' First Impressions of Website Aesthetics With a Quantification of Perceived Visual Complexity and Colorfulness
authors: Reinecke, K., Yeh, T., Miratrix, L., Mardiko, R., Zhao, Y., Liu, J., Gajos, K. Z.
key_findings: 450 websites, 548 volunteers; image-feature models predicted perceived colourfulness (R2 .78) and complexity (R2 .65).
Appeal after 500 ms dropped strongly at high complexity and slightly at very low complexity; colourfulness played a minor role.
Age and native language affected appeal; even award-winning sites were disliked by many; model explained ~48% of appeal variance.
practical_applications: Visual complexity is the first lever on a split-second impression; keep complexity low-to-moderate for feed images, and test per audience.
limitations: Website screenshots, online volunteers; does not measure trust or long-term liking.

title: The role of visual complexity and prototypicality regarding first impression of websites: Working towards understanding aesthetic judgments
authors: Tuch, A. N., Presslaber, E. E., Stöcklin, M., Opwis, K., Bargas-Avila, J. A.
key_findings: 119 real website screenshots varying in visual complexity and prototypicality; effects appear within 17-50 ms.
Low complexity + high prototypicality = most beautiful.
Complexity acts earlier; prototypicality's influence grows with viewing time (consistent with Leder's stage model).
practical_applications: For instant impressions: simple and genre-typical first; novelty can be added where viewing time is longer (later slides, captions).
limitations: Websites, lab; preprint version read.

title: Quicker, faster, darker: Changes in Hollywood film over 75 years
authors: Cutting, J. E., Brunick, K. L., DeLong, J. E., Iricinschi, C., Candan, A.
key_findings: 160 English-language films 1935-2010: shots got shorter; more motion; shorter shots carry proportionately more motion in recent films; films got darker (mean frame luminance decreased).
Authors attribute all four trends to filmmakers increasing control of viewer attention; darker images with wider dynamic range allow more contrast control.
practical_applications: 'Cinematic' in contemporary terms correlates with darker overall key, controlled contrast, motivated motion and short shots; use as checkable features, not as a guarantee of quality.
limitations: Hollywood English-language sample; descriptive trends, not audience-preference tests.

title: The Handmade Effect: What's Love Got to Do with It?
authors: Fuchs, C., Schreier, M., van Osselaer, S.
key_findings: Per abstract/press: four studies show handmade products are more attractive, largely because they symbolically 'contain love'; effort, quality, uniqueness, authenticity and pride were controlled.
Effect stronger for gifts to loved ones; press reports willingness to pay up to 17% more.
practical_applications: Visible human making (hands, process, the optician fitting) adds warmth and authenticity, strongest for gift/love framings.
limitations: Full text not read.

title: Humans versus AI: whether and why we prefer human-created compared to AI-created artwork
authors: Bellaiche, L., Shahi, R., Turpin, M. H., Ragnhildstveit, A., Sprockett, S., Barr, N., Christensen, A., Seli, P.
key_findings: All paintings were AI-made; random 'Human-created' vs 'AI-created' labels.
Human-labelled art rated higher on liking, beauty, profundity and worth (Study 1, replicated in Study 2).
Perceived story and effort moderated label effects for liking/beauty; attitudes to AI moderated profundity/worth.
practical_applications: The label/provenance changes judgement independent of pixels; communicate human intent, story and effort when AI tools are used.
limitations: Online samples; paintings not commercial images; label manipulation only.

title: AI-synthesized faces are indistinguishable from real faces and more trustworthy
authors: Nightingale, S. J., Farid, H.
key_findings: 315 participants: accuracy at telling StyleGAN2 faces from real was 48.2% (chance).
With training and trial-by-trial feedback (219 participants): about 59%, no improvement over time.
Trustworthiness: synthetic faces 4.82 vs real 4.48 (small effect).
practical_applications: Photoreal AI faces are not reliably detectable by viewers; 'AI-looking' cues come from styling, lighting and context more than face pixels; disclose honestly.
limitations: 2021-era GAN faces, cropped portraits; not full scenes or products.

title: AI Hyperrealism: Why AI Faces Are Perceived as More Real Than Human Ones
authors: Miller, E. J., et al.
key_findings: Per BPS Research Digest and abstracts: White AI faces were judged human more often than real White faces (N = 124 in Exp 1).
AI faces were more average/less distinctive; people relied on familiarity/memorability cues that did not help; higher attractiveness pointed to AI.
Least accurate participants were most confident / had least insight.
practical_applications: Over-averaged, over-attractive, frictionless faces are a statistical tell of AI imagery; add specific, characterful features.
limitations: Original article not read (403); White faces only effect; Psychological Science 34(12) per summary.

title: AI-generated food stimuli match real counterparts in perceived healthiness and calorie content but not in realism or willingness to eat
authors: Diel, A., et al.
key_findings: 87 participants rated 60 pairs of AI-generated vs validated real food photos.
AI images rated less realistic and lower willingness to eat; healthiness and calorie ratings did not differ.
Relative realism of an AI image predicted its relative healthiness and willingness-to-eat ratings.
practical_applications: AI product imagery can communicate category facts but loses appetite/desire when it looks unreal; realism drives desire.
limitations: Food domain, single online study; participants did not classify AI vs real.

title: Disclaimer! This Content Is AI-Generated: How AI-Disclosures Influence Trust in Advertisements and Organizations
authors: Koning, B., Voorveld, H. A. M.
key_findings: Between-subjects experiment (N = 304): GAI ad with vs without AI disclosure.
Disclosure raised AI knowledge and persuasion knowledge, which mostly lowered trust in the ad and organisation.
A positive indirect path also appeared (via attitudinal persuasion knowledge to higher trust).
practical_applications: Disclosure has a trust cost on average but is ethically and often legally required; pair it with human-intent framing (see Bellaiche2023).
limitations: Single ad, Dutch sample; Journal of Interactive Advertising 25(3).

title: Blinded with Science or Informed by Charts? A Replication Study
authors: Dragicevic, P., Jansen, Y.
key_findings: Per abstract/summary: four replications (total N = 623) of Tal & Wansink's claim that trivial charts make claims more persuasive failed; text with chart was no more (sometimes less) persuasive.
The chart slightly improved understanding.
practical_applications: A 'scientific look' (graphs, formulas) does not reliably add credibility; use charts only when they inform.
limitations: Full text blocked; crowdsourced samples.

title: Are Men Seduced by Red? The Effect of Red Versus Black Prices on Price Perceptions
authors: Puccinelli, N. M., Chandrashekaran, R., Grewal, D., Suri, R.
key_findings: Per abstract: men perceived greater savings when prices were shown in red vs black (low involvement); women showed better price recall.
practical_applications: Red price tags code 'deal/discount': useful for promos, but the same code pulls a premium look toward 'sale/cheap'.
limitations: Full text not read; magnitude figures differ between press sources.
